The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-36, an Act to amend the Advance Payments for Crops Act and the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mr. Foster (p.4275).
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise this afternoon to speak on Bill C-36, an act to amend the Advance Payments for Crops Act and the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act and the amendment to the motion which essentially calls for the bill not to be read at this time but six months from now.
Speaking directly to the amendment, I first want to suggest that postponing this bill for six months is not the effort that farm producers and producer groups would like to see. They would like to see this bill withdrawn completely and the existing act which was in place prior to the April budget of the finance minister be in force so they may have the full weight of the benefits of the advance payments act which existed prior to this year.
To clarify that a little further, the bill before us today essentially brings into practice what the Minister of Finance announced in the budget in April of this year, that the government would no longer pay interest on advances for the purchase of grain. The argument raised, of course, is that the government would rather use the $27 million expended on this program than have the producers in the field use it.
Farm groups, of course, have said the advances are important because they allow producers to sell their crops when the prices are high, when they are in the bins and they cannot sell them, and I will elaborate on that a little bit more in a few minutes.
We have to remember that this program was brought in in 1957 and has served the farm community extremely well since then. The farm population has utilized the program and has found it to be of great benefit. The fact that the government is now in financial difficulties is no reason to penalize the farm community which oft-times have no other place to turn than this particular program.
There are a couple of things that I should mention. This program is extremely valuable at times like this when the agriculture community is in such a state of stress. The financial crisis in the farm sector is absolutely real. It is having an impact right down to the human level. In some cases farmers have taken their lives because they felt that they failed their fathers' generation, their fathers who had broken the land and had often lost hands or legs while building up the country and producing on the land for their children. Then their children come along, and because of policies of the previous government and this government, they can no

October 5, 1989
Government Orders
longer maintain their farms. Some of those farmers feel that they have failed their fathers and their grandfathers, and their sense of being has been destroyed.
The crisis is very real and we will remember a few things. We have to remember that this government is pushing more and more of the costs on to the farmers and they are getting absolutely no support from this government in terms of raising the price of the product. My colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt earlier today talked about the prices for farm products and he is absolutely right. Bills like this one before us today would be unnecessary if the price paid for farm products was adequate to meet the needs of the farm community.
Other programs that this government boasts about would be unnecessary if the price paid for the farm product was adequate to meet the needs of the production. A lot of the farm community is looking for that opportunity to indeed be carrying the weight of the economy. This is not the time to be pushing more and more costs on the producer.
I just want to remind you, Mr. Speaker, and some of the government members here today of what is happening out there in the farm community and why interest free cash advances are so important.
We know that the price is down on almost all commodities. Therefore, with the price down and support from the government down, obviously farm income is down, but interest rates remain very high. We cannot forget that the previous government had interest rates up to 20 per cent and 22 per cent and that is what forced many of the people in the farm community to get into this crisis situation.
Input costs continue to increase. With the free trade legislation and the goods and services tax being brought in, all of those input costs are increasing at the farm level. The expenses rise, the price continues to fall, and more and more of the costs of doing business are being transferred to the farmer.
We cannot forget that earlier this year oats was removed by this government from the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board. Subsequent to that move, the price of oats has fallen dramatically.
There was no stabilization payment for grains this year, even though in a period of time like this one
following a drought, stabilization payments are more important than ever. Do not forget the deficiency payments that the Minister of Agriculture has been so proud of have been stopped, and there was not a dollar of deficiency payments made to any producer last year or this year.
The rail line rehabilitation program has also been terminated, meaning that more and more producers are going to have to haul their grain further and further to the elevator. Again, the cost of that transportation cost has been pushed over on to the farmer, and there is absolutely no support for the increased price that is paid for that product.
I can go on. I am going to list just a few other things here. We have to remember that the compensation payment that this government promised after it took away the two price wheat system last year because of the free trade deal has disappeared, and $270 million was promised, a one-time payment for a price that has been paid for years and years and years on the use of domestic grain in Canada. It disappeared.
The Minister of Agriculture was in Prince Albert not too long ago talking about crop insurance and how the crop insurance program that this government is going to implement is going to be the salvation of the agriculture community. Crop insurance is a very important aspect of the farm price circumstances, but the crop insurance system is not the end all answer to supporting the income of the farmer and certainly not if the farmer has to come up with higher and higher premiums every year just in order to stay in that program.
Too many of the people in the farm community are on the line. They have just barely enough cash flow, if any, to go from one year to the next. Interest and expenses cut into that cash flow significantly and we cannot increase that in any way.
One of the things that I discovered this summer as I worked more and more closely with labour market conditions in my own riding and as I looked around the province of Saskatchewan, was that Canada Employment Centres across the prairies are indicating that there is a tremendous lack of skilled farm labourers available at harvest time. Not only do the producers have to pull off these crops with more and more expensive equipment, because of course the cost of this stuff has all been increasing, but they are having to utilize it with less and less skilled labour. It is becoming a tremendous problem
October 5, 1989

throughout the prairies and particularly in Saskatchewan.
Last, I mentioned the significance of cash flow on the farm. The goods and services tax proposed by this government is going to just destroy that cash flow position of the farmer or the producer on the western prairies. We can be sure that when the people in the farm communities start to look at all of these things, decisions made by government which could be made in another way that are affecting their lives, their ability to produce food from the land, they are certainly going to have second thoughts about the way in which they direct their attention in the future.
Two days ago in the House of Commons, the Minister of Agriculture spoke to us and he had a number of interesting things to say about this bill. I would like to make a few comments on what he had to say.
You will recall that he was talking about the opposition holding up this legislation. Here we are into the harvest, in fact the harvest in Saskatchewan is over. The grain is in the farmers' bins and they are looking for ways to sell it. In fact, if you go out and look at those bins you will find that a lot of them are full of grain. If you go to the grain elevators you will find that they are also full. The elevators cannot take any more of the grain that is in the bins but the farmer has to sell that grain.
This government is forcing that farmer now to take an advance on grain he can't sell and actually borrow the money for the sale and pay back interest. A number of those producers are sitting there with grain that the board is not buying at this time, grain which, because we had poor weather in the fall, is now fit for feed instead of export. That grain is not going to be bought for transport now. The grain that is being purchased now by the elevators is used for our exports, our best quality grain.
So the farmer who is sitting there with feed grain is wondering how he can go to the elevator and get paid for the grain that he has grown without having to borrow the money, which is what this government is now asking him to do. I am afraid this is a situation that is intolerable and shows the ignorance of this government about the conditions on the farm and how things work.
Government Orders
Before I come back to the Minister of Agriculture I have to mention a statement made yesterday by the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds. He said the major hold-up in all of this is because farmers out there don't want to haul their grain in winter. He said:
There is no point in the guy hauling in the middle of winter because it is 40 below and he does not want to start his tractor, blow out the lane, get his truck going and all that. He has got his money. But if he has got to haul the grain to get his money, that helps as far as orderly marketing.
Well, I am sure there isn't a farmer out there who is going to read that statement, think about last winter when the weather was 40 below, and think "Oh, if I had not got my money then I would have shovelled out my driveway, shovelled out the road, got out to the elevator and delivered my grain because I needed the money." That is not the nature of this at all. What we are talking about is selling product when you can sell it and not having to borrow the money because the grain is in the bin and there is nothing you can do about it.
The Minister of Agriculture boasts that the limits have moved up from some $30,000 to $250,000. Big deal, Mr. Speaker. When you are not paying the bill you could put that up to $500,000, make it a million dollar limit. When you are not footing the bill it makes no difference. They can claim all the credit they want on this one for boosting the limits, but when you are borrowing the money at the producer level it doesn't make any difference on that side. It is still a loan and it is still a transfer of the cost to the producer. As I have indicated, the producer at this point does not need those additional costs.
We can't forget that the payments that were going into this program before amounted to some $27 million. When you look at the western economy, $27 million out of that economy, no matter how you look at it, is a lot.
I also want to make a suggestion. Earlier in the House today it was said that only a few farmers take advantage of this program, this is becoming more and more typical of this government. The government says that only a few use it so it is okay.
That is what the government says about the VIA Rail users. While this debate is going on, the same debate on VIA Rail is taking place. Only 3 per cent of the Canadian population use VIA Rail so slash it by 51 per cent. What an attitude!

October 5, 1989
Government Orders
The Government may say it is only a few. I do not care whether it is a few. I know it is not a few, not for farm producers and not for VIA Rail users. Those are important people and important parts of our society which deserve the support that they have been getting both on VIA Rail and particularly on this bill, the Advance Payments Act. These people, the producers and travellers, are not expendable in our economy.
My colleague last night in the House of Commons also suggested that the government, if you want to extend this logic any further, will next be closing down heart support units in this country because only a few people use those as well. I am afraid that, as disgusting as that thought may be, I tend to agree with the suggestion.
The Minister of Agriculture also talked about how the budget cuts have to extend through to the farm sector, and said that the government was not walking away from supporting the farmers of Canada. He is very proud of the distinguished record that the government has had in the past. Again I say, "Oh yeah, some record". We just recognized that we have the most serious financial crisis in agriculture in the history of this country and this government is bragging about all that it has done. It may have put more money into agriculture than any previous government, but that tells me one thing, that no previous government has supported agriculture properly or adequately, and, secondly, because the crisis is still there, that no matter what it has done to this point, it has not been adequate, it has not changed the problem, it has not helped get producers from one time to another.
We still have producers throughout the prairies who are looking to that great crop next year because that is what they need to survive. There have been so many things that have been pushing them down that there is every reason for the Saskatchewan producers to continue to believe that they do live in "next year country". Unfortunately, as long as governments take positions like this, it is always going to be next year country in Saskatchewan because there is nothing that is going to help to get them ahead.
I want to make one more comment on a quote made by the Minister of Agriculture. He said:
We are asking the agriculture sector to do its share and to help
overcome Canada's deficit problems. Farmers, like other Canadians,
in the long run will benefit from the action we are taking today to put
this country on a sounder financial footing.
Wonderful words, Mr. Speaker, but what he is saying is that the farmers who are left may benefit from the programs that are put in place by this government. I would suggest that there will certainly be no benefit at the farm community level for any of the producers who are sitting there now and dealing with the crisis that has been perpetuated by this and the previous government.
Over the last little while I have had numerous representations from individual fanners within my own riding and from various producer and commodity groups across the country. A number of those groups have suggested that we have to do everything we can to convince this government to maintain the interest free part of the advance payments act. Those groups are wide-ranging across the board, from those who are active in my province to those who are active across the country.
Obviously they have made those pleas to the government on the opposite side of the House. Both ministers who have spoken in this debate, the Minister of Grain and Oilseeds and the Minister of Agriculture, have discounted what they have been told by these major farm organizations. I am afraid I find that much too similar to the other activities that are going on. The government is not listening to the people on the goods and services tax, it is not listening to the people on VIA Rail, and now it is not listening to the interest groups that are active in the industry.
I have information before me from the Ontario Soybean Growers Marketing Board, the Com Growers Association, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Canadian Wheat Board Advisory Committee, the National Farmers' Union and many others, all of whom are saying, maintain the interest free portion of the cash advance. It is crucial to the western farmers to keep the cash flow and keep the grain flowing from the farmer to the elevator to the export market.
I thank you for the opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to speak in this afternoon's debate and I wish the government well in pursuing its agriculture policies in the future.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to commend my friend from The Battlefords-Meadow Lake. I have listened with great interest to what he has had to say. Many in this chamber will think of fish when
October 5, 1989

they see me rise in my place because much of my riding depends so heavily on the fishery and I spend a fair amount of my time in this chamber talking about that.
There are two important agricultural pockets in the riding of Burin-St. George's. One is called the Codroy Valley, a very agriculturally fertile valley where there is a farming segment extending up into the Robinsons area. The other is on the Burin peninsula, the Winterland area in particular. So in my riding of Burin-St. George's there is some concern about farming matters generally.
I rise, not only because I am proud to represent farmers in this House, but for another reason. I want to put a question to the member and in so doing state my second reason for rising. The amendment by my friend, the member for Algoma, seconded by my seatmate and friend and colleague from Lambton-Middlesex, has the solution to this problem and I am wondering whether the gentleman from The Battlefords-Meadow Lake shares our view on what the solution is.
The existing legislation adequately addresses the problem. I heard a gentleman on the Tory back-bench today rave on about how the big bad Liberals and NDPers were holding up things and keeping money from the farmers. Let us keep the record straight on this. The existing statute allows the advance payments to flow. This legislation that we are now debating would put some restrictions on it, would make the amounts more measly and would introduce the question of interest and so on.
We understand what the Tories want to do, because we see a pattern here. It is the same thing they are trying to do to the fishermen. It is the same thing they are doing on VIA Rail, on Canada Post, on the Canada job development program.
If you want an umbrella phrase for all these apparently diverse issues, the umbrella phrase is "Chinese water torture". They are now doing to farmers what they have been doing to the fishermen for a long time, what they are doing to postal recipients in rural Newfoundland and rural Canada generally. They are sending out the message as part of the Tory agenda that if you live anywhere
Government Orders
other than the Torontos, Vancouvers and Montreals of this world, we do not need you.
And so by a process, a slow Chinese water torture process, they are sending the message to farmers, aided and abetted by Tories who represent, however temporarily, farm ridings, to fishermen in rural Newfoundland and all parts of the Atlantic and the B.C. coast, through the Chinese water torture approach, that you are not part of our agenda, you are not part of the mainstream because you do not live in Toronto and you are not middle income. That is what this bill is all about. It is another step in the process, another cog in the wheel, another effort, another sequence in the Chinese water torture.
So I rise to put a question to my friend from The Battlefords-Meadow Lake. Does he not see in this bill an effort by the Tories to put the farmer just a little further underfoot? Also, does he not support the amendment put down by my friend from Algoma, and seconded by the gentleman from Lambton-Middlesex, that would give this whole thing a six month hoist, get it off the chamber floor, and let the fanners know where they stand on this so the government, under existing statute, can send out the payments as it should be doing instead of monkeying around with this cowardly bill here in the House in the first place?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague from Newfoundland for the question. Before I answer the question he raised, I would like to comment on the closeness of the people of Newfoundland and Saskatchewan. They are very much like close cousins. Newfoundlanders have the ocean and we have our oceans of wheat that wave and blow in the breeze. We also have producers who rely on seasonal conditions to maintain their entire economy. The price of wheat and fish, the quotas day. Neither the producers in Newfoundland nor the producers in Saskatchewan have any control over their ability to maintain their life from year to year or from day to day.
The hand of government is heavy on the people who live in Newfoundland and Saskatchewan. In that regard, we have a tremendous amount in common. I have great respect for all those who come from Newfoundland and I hope and trust that they have the same for people from Saskatchewan.

October 5, 1989
Government Orders
The member talked a lot about the existing legislation and I agree. I thought I made it clear in my speech that the existing legislation which has been in place since 1957 has been very good to the producers in this regard. The interest free advance payment is just fine.
The problem with the amendment put forward by his colleague in the Liberal Party is that it does not ask or request or demand that the government actually implement the existing legislation or bring in the statutes that are required from it. The government has stated very clearly that there is nothing available for producers. If we stall this bill there will continue to be nothing in place until such time as the government decides what it wants to do. Until we get that commitment and something that guarantees that the interest free portion of this act will continue I will have difficulty supporting the amendment even though I agree that the change has to be made.
I would like to make one other thing clear, Mr. Speaker. During the time I had allocated to me I did not get a chance to specifically tie the reason for implementing this bill to the economic conditions in the country, namely, what the Conservative government sees as the big problem, the deficit. I maintain that if this government was serious about combating the deficit in Canada it would not be doing it on the backs of farmers, it would be hauling the Bank of Canada in here before us and demanding that the interest rates in this country be lowered. Until that happens, none of these other things will make a great deal of difference.

Mr. Speaker, the poetic interventions of our colleagues from Newfoundland and Saskatchewan are a tough act to follow. However, I am pleased to rise today in the House to speak on Bill C-36, an Act to amend the Advance Payments for Crops Act and the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act.
I would like to begin by congratulating my colleagues from Algoma and Lambton-Middlesex for the excellent interventions they have made on this bill. I would hope that the government will listen as well to the points they have raised and listen to the many farmers of this country who also oppose this bill.
The government must realize that Bill C-36 is both counterproductive and harmful to Canadian agriculture. Many members of this House have received a considerable amount of correspondence from various national
and provincial agricultural organizations regarding Bill C-36. I have received letters from groups such as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Ontario Soybean Growers Marketing Board and the Ontario Com Producers Association. Each and every one of these organizations are against the passage of Bill C-36. Obviously organizations such as these are aware of the needs of farmers and are aware of what actions the federal government should or should not take in order to ensure the success of Canadian agriculture. These groups have outlined several reasons why Bill C-36 should not be passed. I suggest that groups such as those I have mentioned have put forward valid arguments as to why Bill C-36 should not be passed. Unfortunately, the federal government in its infinite wisdom seems willing to ignore the views of the expert voices of Canadian agriculture.
One of the main reasons why farm groups do not wish to see Bill C-36 pass is that the bill eliminates the interest free provision of the cash advance program. These interest free advances are important factors in maintaining market stability in particular agriculture sectors. By eliminating the interest free portion of the advance payment for crops program the value of the entire program and its use by farmers will be reduced.
The advance payment for crops is a vital avenue for supplying farmers with the necessary funds to pay their operating costs and purchase supplies. It enables farmers to be in a position where they are not forced to sell their crops at harvest time when the market is flooded and prices are low. The advance payment for crops program has traditionally played a vital role in assisting farmers in the planning of their operations for the crop year. By cancelling the interest free provision of this program the government will place farmers in a difficult situation. They will no longer be able to rely on the fiscal and market stability which existed previously.
The interest free portion of the program enabled producers to store their crops at harvest time and still pay their bills and buy supplies for the coming crop year. This program has provided farmers with the flexibility to sell their crops at a time when the market price was high so they could meet financial obligations and prepare for the crop year ahead. The market also avoided being flooded at harvest and avoided shortages later on. Thus
October 5, 1989

both the producer and agriculture benefited by this program.
With Bill C-36 all this will change. Farmers will have to pay interest costs on the advance payments. This added financial outlay will be expensive and detrimental to the usefulness of the program. With interest rates being as high as they are the financial burden to farmers who participate in this revamped program will be considerable. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has already stated that the elimination of the interest free portion of the program takes away one of the few avenues farmers have to deal effectively with high interest rates.
The Ontario com producers argue that while the federal guarantee under the ACPA will allow farmers to borrow money at, or slightly below the prime interest rate, administration charges would mean an actual cost to producers at well above prime. This, in effect, will provide no advantage over commercial sources of credit. The elimination of the interest free provision will effectively destroy the program and result in an ineffectual program with minimal participation. This even if the current advance loan levels are significantly increased as provided for in Bill C-36.
By eliminating the interest free provision of the advance payments program the government will not accomplish too much toward addressing the federal deficit. The government states it will save $27 million in the 1989-90 and 1990-91 crop years by not having to pay the interest on the cash advances to farmers. However, the government will at the same time create an agricultural sector with reduced farm incomes and a weakened marketing structure.
Furthermore, a number of farm organizations have argued that the relative cost of the APCA marketing program has been minimal when compared to the benefits the program established in the agricultural sector. The program was a useful one for producers and it achieved its intended goal of creating an orderly marketing system for the crops involved.
This program benefited farmers and the agriculture industry alike. Why then, if the program was such a success and the costs comparatively minor compared to the benefits produced, does the federal government now want to eliminate the interest free provision? Such a decision is illogical and completely inconsistent with this
Government Orders
government's promises to support Canadian agriculture and Canadian farmers.
It is worth remembering the untenable situation which existed in agriculture prior to the advance payment for crops program coming into effect. Farmers sold their crops at harvest time when crop prices were traditionally low as they had no choice if they were to address their financial obligations.
The selling of crops at harvest created supply and demand imbalances and brought about price cutting and predatory marketing. The Advance Payments for Crops Act was viewed as an important remedy to these serious problems.
In a very real way the government is now planning to turn back the clock by disposing of the interest free provision of the program. If Bill C-36 passes, farmers will be charged interest on the advance payments they receive for their produce. The net result is higher costs for producers and a depressed price for their produce in an unstable market system.
If the government proceeds with Bill C-36 it will be displaying the lack of concern it has for farmers who have relied upon the interest free provisions of the program. The government will display its callous attitude toward maintaining a strong and effective marketing system for crops and it will also display its unwillingness to assist and support Canadian agriculture.
The situation in Canadian agriculture today is not one which instils a lot of confidence. Many farmers believe that the future of supply management in Canada is being threatened. Recent Canada-U.S. conflicts over yoghurt and ice cream as well as pork when added to the other problems such as industrial milk prices and the agricultural talks at the GATT, have generated a feeling among farmers that they cannot rely upon the government to assist and support their industry. Now the government wishes to cut the interest free part of the advance payments program. One can easily understand why our farmers feel the way they do.
The governments of other countries have not instituted similar actions in areas relating to programs such as advance payments for crops. The United States have their storage loans programs and Europeans have their intervention purchases which maintain commodity prices in the European community. These governments maintain interest free provisions in their respective programs.

October 5, 1989
Government Orders
They have not indicated any plans to transfer the interest paying burden to their producers.
The GATT Geneva Accord of April, 1989 calls upon countries such as Canada to freeze existing support programs. This accord does not force Canada to remove the interest free provisions of programs such as the APCA. Thus, there is no international pressure upon the Canadian government to remove the interest free aspect of the program.
It cannot be said that the advance payments for crops program is trade distorting. It isn't. The program does not stimulate production, it merely encourages and fosters orderly marketing of crops and grains. Thus, there is no conflict with either the program itself or the interest free provisions with regard to international trade.
I believe it is time for the government to show Canadian farmers that they are still important to the country. The advance payments for crops program was designed to assist farmers and facilitate effective marketing. By watering down the effectiveness of the program both farmers and agriculture in general will come out the loser.
I would like this government to start implementing responsible initiatives in agriculture rather than putting forward legislation such as Bill C-36.1 urge the Minister of Agriculture to use the existing Advance Payments for Crops Act and Prairie Grains Advance Payments Act legislation and sign the agreements with producer organizations for this crop year. The minister must surely be aware that the harvest period has been completed in western Canada and is proceeding in other areas of the country. Farmers deserve to know what is in store for them.
The government would like us to believe that the interest free aspect of the advance payments given to farmers is not a fundamental part of the program's over-all objective of providing cash in advance on the strength of marketable crops. I would argue that having the interest free provision assists the farmers in the ways I have already discussed and is, in fact, vital toward assisting in the maintenance of an orderly marketing system.
This in itself is enough to view the interest free provision as being quite important to the over-all program.
It is expected that this measure to remove the interest free provision will lead to higher interest costs for farmers, with the increased cost dependent on interest rates and other dimensions of the loan packages arranged by farm organizations. Some of these organizations in western Canada have predicted that borrowing costs will increase by some $1,500 to $2,000 per farm per year. This is indeed a significant cost for producers to bear especially with the high interest rates currently in effect.
With regard to grain, Bill C-36 may cause increased congestion in a shrinking elevator system as farmers deliver early in order to receive payment. Thus, there will be added pressure on grain companies to ensure shipping points have adequate storage facilities. This is yet another example of the problems Bill C-36 will create.
Some producers believe that the orderly marketing of grains may be hampered as a result of Bill C-36. A number of agricultural groups believe that these cash advances have facilitated grain marketing, enabling grain to move smoothly through the system. Bill C-36 may well lead to increased pressures for high quotas early in the year.
Grain and oilseed producers have already paid their share to deficit reduction with the phasing out of excise and sales tax exemptions on diesel fuel and gasoline used in food production. I guess the government wants to go one better and have these producers shoulder more of the burden.
In conclusion, we can clearly see the harm Bill C-36 will cause if it is passed. It will have a negative effect upon com and soybean producers in Ontario and grain producers in western Canada. Our farmers deserve better support from their federal government. They deserve to have the interest free advance payments for crops program and an orderly market system.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas would share his thoughts on the security of our food supply in view of the demise of the fishing industry and the severe downturn in the farming industry.
October 5, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for her question and particularly for her concern as I know it is a source of serious concern for her and for all of us in the House. I would not leave out anyone in the House. I think it is a concern of national interest to all of us.
In speaking with many producers in Stormont-Dun-das, many of whom have family ties that originate from European countries such as Holland, they speak from past experiences within their own families in their original homelands. They have tried to impress upon me on many occasions that Canada should never leave itself vulnerable in such a critical area.
I think it would be callous of any government not to protect the security of each and every Canadian by maintaining a supply of food necessary to feed each and every one in the nation. I think we have to go one step better because it is expected of us by the international community, living in a rich country as we do, benefiting from the vast agricultural lands and so on.
We are certainly well placed to assist the international community where many people in various countries have far less than we do. Canadians have and will continue to show not only their respect but their generosity to all peoples of this world. We should be able to assist increasingly in feeding people around the world.
In closing, I thank my colleague again for raising the very important concern that she and all of us have.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this measure which is very close to my constituents and very close to myself. It has been an important part of western Canada's ability to keep grains on the market.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, this measure would amend two acts, one of which is the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act and the second which is the Advance Payments for Crops Act. These two acts service two very specific parts of the country. The Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act services the area of Canada which produces wheat, barley, and it used to for oats, those areas which are under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. The Canadian Wheat Board is the administrative body for this particular act.
Government Orders
The Advance Payments for Crops Act covers almost all other crops designated across the country. There are people in almost every province of Canada who have taken advantage of this act. In British Columbia, 1,000 people took advantage of it. In Prince Edward Island, where I think the amount is not quite so large, 214 people took advantage of it in 1987-88. The total who took advantage of the act in 1987-88 was close to 10,000 farmers.
The Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act serviced a good many more than that. Twenty per cent or 25 per cent on occasion, sometimes higher, of the farmers in western Canada who hold permit books have taken advantage of the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act.
Right now, in both of those areas, there are farmers in crisis situations. In fact, in rural Canada-and I am not speaking entirely of agricultural rural Canada-forestry, fishing and agriculture are in crisis positions. Therefore it is very difficult to understand why this government which claims to be so concerned about the welfare of the agricultural community should choose at this time to withdraw from this particular field. This withdrawal amounts to approximately $40,000 out of the pockets of the farmers of western Canada in this year in interest to the loans that they could have made. As far as the Advance Payments for Crops Act is concerned, it is my understanding that very few people will find it of value if they have to pay interest for their loans.
The reason for these two acts is interesting. The history should be known as part of the debate on this issue. The Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act was put in place by the Diefenbaker government in 1957. At that time we in the prairies were having difficulty in getting our grain to market. We were having difficulty storing it and the world did not need our grain in the fall. So the Diefenbaker government put in place the Prairie Grains Advance Payments Act which allowed the farmer to get some of the money for his crop. It actually enabled the farmer to sell some of his crop. When he delivered the grain to the elevator later on, that portion of the loan was taken from the crop he delivered.
Once it was in place, the government, the farmers and the grain industry recognized that this had far-reaching benefits because it allowed a spread-out of grain deliveries across the year. It allowed the Wheat Board to not

October 5, 1989
Government Orders
get a huge amount of delivery in the fall. It allowed the delivery of grain to be spread out so that they could supply the world market in a more orderly manner.
Because the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act operated so well, in 1977 the government brought in the second act, the Advance Payments for Crops Act. This was essentially brought in to cover crops in eastern Canada. However, it now covers crops in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and Prince Edward Island. It covers those crops that are not under supply-management and those crops that are not under the Wheat Board.
The primary purpose of the Advance Payments for Crops Act was to encourage orderly marketing. It has been very successful in doing that. This government has a penchant to deliver to the marketing structure rather than to allow security for the farmers or the producers of variety products. Their bible, if you wish to say that, is the market system. The market system, however, in agriculture always seemed to pay less in the fall when we had the crop. Then, after you had delivered it, the prices started to go up. When you did not have any grain or any crop to deliver in the spring or in the mid-winter, the prices were high.
The act allowed the farmer to hold the crop in his bin, get some money to pay his bills and then sell it at the higher market. It worked well. It worked for the benefit of the farmer, but it also worked for the benefit of the processors and the products that were handled in the industry, because it spread the delivery over a long period of time.
The government says that it is urgent that it get this bill through. How is it urgent? There is an act in place. If the legislation is in place which would allow this government to provide interest free loans to the western grain producers, if they wanted it, and interest free loans to the producers of other crops across Canada, there is a statutory requirement in place that all they have to do is make the move and the money will become available. Nobody here or in the country believes that they could not do that and could not make that money available very quickly if they really felt strongly about getting this money out to the farmers at this time.
The reason the Minister of Agriculture gave for the change in the act was the deficit. The cost of this program, about $40 million, is about $20 million out of the farmers' pockets this year and another possible total of $100 million over the next crop year. This total would be the cost to the government. It is not much of a contribution to the deficit, yet it is a tremendous amount to take out of the pockets of individual farmers.
Over the years it has become quite obvious that in agriculture, along with fisheries and forestry, rural Canada needs some kind of structure in place which allows sustainability, which allows those parts of Canada that are dependent upon those industries to remain productive and viable. These two acts were a very small part of a structure which attempted to do that. What we need is something much larger and much more secure than these two acts. But these two acts were there and gave the farmers the kind of support they needed when they needed it.
We have a tendency to say that this is support to the farmers. It is much more than that because the farmers across Canada get their supplies, usually on credit, from the small villages, the towns or even the cities around which they live. They buy their inputs from those areas on credit. When they get these advance payments, they are able to pay their bills. They are able to pay their bills without increasing their debt burden.
One of the things that everybody in Canada knows is that the debt burden of people in agriculture is huge. The total debt for agriculture across Canada right now is something over $23 billion.
What the government is asking these farmers to do, because it is the farmers who are already short of cash and who will make these loans, is to add on to that debt and increase the possibility of them going under. The possibility of them being foreclosed on or going under is veiy real.
In my province alone there are over 10,000 farmers right now being served with foreclosure notices, foreclosure notices which will take part of their land, part of their machinery or affect them in some way. Those are only the notices that we know about, the changes in ownership and structure of the rural community that we know about. A lot of farmers just throw up their hands and sign a quit claim which allows them to turn over, with a certain amount of saving of face, their farm or part
October 5, 1989

of their farm and either rent it back or let somebody else farm it for the next few years.
We have a disastrous situation, a crisis situation on the farm these days. We have a government which says: "We want to save a little more money and this is one place where we can save it", at the expense of the farmer.
The point has been made often today and before that it is not a large number of people. It might not be a large number of people, but it is a fair sized group. As I pointed out before, the number of people in 1987-88 who made use of the Advance Payments for Crops Act across the country was something around 10,000 farmers. The number of people who made use of the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act was approximately 20 per cent of the 150,000 fanners who have quota books.
It is not as if this is a small group. Of course, it is the group that needs it most, in most cases. I know, and the government can point to this I am sure, that there are people who make use of these acts who do not need it. However, it would be very simple to put into the applications for advance payment some requirement which would at least force them to tell the producer organization, which in many cases is made up of their friends and neighbours, whether or not they had a cash flow problem. I am sure that the supplier down the road could tell you right now which of the farmers in the community have a cash flow problem and which ones do not and, therefore, which ones need advance payment and which do not.
I reiterate, this is not the time to move away from interest free advance payments. This is not the time to move into something which puts the farmer in a position where he has one more burden to worry about.
I support wholly the hoist motion which was moved by the member for Algoma which suggests that we forget about this bill now and look at it again six months from now. I would much rather of course see the government withdraw this bill now and put into effect the present legislation which would allow, within the next month or to, the bringing in of supplementary estimates, if they wish-they say they do not have any money in the
Government Orders
budget-which would allow them to cover the loans that might be made.
This government has, over the years, suggested that they do everything by consultation, that they are very good at consultation. We have had a number of farm organizations that have questioned that. They said: "Yes, they come to us and they tell us what they are going to do. They leave and do what they want". They do not consider that consultation. In this particular case had they consulted with the farm producer groups across Canada-and those farm producer groups are a crosssection of the agricultural community and include the Prince Edward Island Potato Marketing Board, the Prince Edward Island Grain Growers, the Corn Growers of Ontario, the Ontario Com Producers Association, the Ontario Soybean Growers Marketing Board-maybe they did consult and went ahead, as usual, doing what they intended-they would have found that there would be no support for the removal of the interest free portion of these acts.
The government has suggested that one of the reasons why it changed the act was to increase the levels, which were $30,000, $60,000 and $90,000.1 suggest, first, that it is very easy to do this if you are borrowing the money and not having to pay the interest on it yourself. Second, this is a pretty good indication that the people they are worried about are the top level people who may not need this in the first place. It is the small fanner who made good use of this and would continue to make good use of this.
I support fully the hoist motion that this bill be put aside for six months and be brought back and, in the meantime, that the present legislation be continued.

Private Members' Business

Mr. Speaker, I believe the hon. member who made that motion is in order, but it would have to come from an urbanite like that to slander the farmers of this country. I, too, live in a large city, but I would like to stand up in my comments and questions to tip my hat to the farmers and the food producers of this country.
Hear, hear!
They are the hardest working and most efficient food producers in the world.
Hear, hear!

With markets around the world becoming so competitive, we should be doing everything within our power to help our farmers stay competitive and be more competitive. What is this government doing? It is doing everything in its power to pull our farmers under.
I would like to ask the member for Saskatoon-Humboldt what the trend is in his riding because I drove through there this summer visiting places like Kuroki, Wadena, Watrous, Wishart, Wynard, all the way to Saskatoon. I am sure his riding touches many of these towns.

Member whether that trend is still continuing or are we saving the family farm. Is the trend of abandoning farms still continuing?

Mr. Speaker, as I pointed out earlier, in my province, even very close to my home constituency in that area where the member was travelling, in some cases as much as 75 per cent of the farmers in some communities have received foreclosure notices and are in the process of losing part or all of their land. They may keep on farming it for a couple of years, but in the end it will go out of the family. It usually goes to somebody else. It means consolidation. The lands will continue to be farmed but by fewer people.
If we had in place a structure which would guarantee a fair price cost of production return on the products which are produced, we would have a viable and an economic industry right across Canada, particularly on the prairies.
