That in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of undertaking research on the cumulative or combined effects of food additives and pest-control products in the Canadian food supply.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on an issue that dramatically illustrates the connection between concerns for the environment, human health, and the connections between those two things and economic decisions.
October 5, 1989

As the critic for health for the New Democrats I have been advocating the restructuring of our health care system to emphasize preventive measures. A full program of preventive care requires that no government decision be taken without integrating concern for human health into the equation.
To me this is a logical step to take along with my party's expressed support for sustainable economic development as set out in a valuable study recently completed by my colleague from Skeena, entitled "Towards a Sustainable Future".
As a species dependent on the earth for our mental and physical well-being, environmental issues are at the same time health issues. It is becoming increasingly clear that by destroying the environment, we create health risks. Destruction of ozone leads to skin cancer; lead emission from car exhausts cause cancer; global warming affects growth patterns causing food shortages and so on. The list is a long one, as we all know.
The issue is not simply protecting the environment. The issue is protecting ourselves. The topic of food additives and the use of pesticides integrates the environment and human health into economic decisions. The misuse of pesticides as we know can destroy wildlife and damage water systems. The accumulation of chemicals in the food supply is increasingly becoming a health hazard.
It is my belief that most members of this House support the goals of reducing our dependence on chemicals and ensuring the highest possible standards in our food supply. Of course taking this approach will give rise to expenditures of money at a time when all initiatives are being sacrificed by this government on the altar of deficit reduction. Those who place government austerity above measures to protect our environment should be looking over their shoulders. Most Canadians are willing to pay to protect the environment and their health. They are showing a greater willingness to vote on the basis of those concerns. Even food suppliers, and Provigo is a good example, are beginning the process of responding to that demand by agreeing to disclose all pesticides used on produce they sell. So while business is responding to these things it appears the government it is not doing all that it might.
Private Members' Business
I encourage the Standing Committee on the Environment to continue the work started in the last Parliament on pesticide use. In particular, the review could be of assistance in encouraging public participation and public information in the ongoing debate over pesticide use. In particular, the ongoing review by the Pesticide Registration Review Secretariat, which I welcome, should be accompanied by the greatest possible public participation. The review could allow for public hearings next year to cover the whole pesticide debate. Involvement of the Environment Committee could ensure that wide attention is brought to the efforts of the secretariat and pressure this government to clean up pesticide registration, the control process, and the enforcement process.
There are two points that I think the Review Secretariat might pay particular attention to. The first relates to concerns voiced in a very wide-spread manner about risk benefit analysis versus risk assessment. In terms of risk benefit analysis generally what is at stake is the risk, for example, the risk to our health against the economic benefit on the part of producers. That sort of economic trade-off has given rise to considerable problems over the last little while and given rise to considerable concern about the use of pesticides and chemical additives in our food.
The second point the Review Secretariat might want to pay particular attention to is that there is no public participation in the whole process of licensing and enforcement. There is not adequate information on decisions which are made and the reasons for those decisions, nor of the health and environmental data used in considering the registration of pesticides.
Canadians are concerned about pesticides and the dangers associated with them, and with the dangers associated with other chemical residues in our food. There is considerable concern in Canada now with the safety of our food supply.
The use of pesticides is widespread. They are sprayed on fruits and vegetables and on other plants to kill parasites, fungi, and weeds. They help protect produce from bruising; they ripen it and give it a better colour; and they are used to control parasites that bother farm animals. As a result, they show up further down in the food chain in the meat we eat. They are a pervasive presence in our food supply.

October 5, 1989
Private Members' Business
The issue has been treated as one of balance, of balancing the health interests of Canadians against the economic interests of producers and manufactures of food and of importers and retailers of food.
There are those who express an optimistic view of the effect of pesticides and chemical additives. Among those, is Dr. Losos, director general of the laboratory centre for disease control of the health protection branch of Health and Welfare Canada who says:
No one can state for certain that anyone ever got cancer as a result
of eating something that contained pesticide residues.
Such a cavalier approach to the problem is counteracted by the fact that some 10,000 cases of bacterial food poisoning are reported to health and welfare each year. I think we have to be concerned about the effects on the health of Canadians of these additives and pesticides. We must put safety and health first. We must ensure that we do not risk the health and safety of Canadians. We must reduce the damage we are doing to our environment.
Scientific opinion recognizes that virtually all pesticides are toxic, at least to some degree. Much of the debate to date has been about the setting of limits and the process by which limits are set.
Pesticides play a vital role in modem agriculture, but there are concerns about dangers to users, the environment, and consumers. Many chemicals and derivative compounds apparently in use are carcinogenic, and other chemicals can have neurotoxic effects and can alter neurological functions.
Food is highly likely to contain some level of pesticide residues. In fact, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 1987 found that 50 per cent of all fruit samples had detectable levels of pesticides. There is no safe level. Regulators cannot guarantee safety and cannot guarantee that no harm is occurring. Instead, we talk of risk benefit. Does the benefit of the product, usually economic, outweigh the probable harm in terms of health of the user, in terms of health of the consumer?
The objective of the process of regulation should be to ensure that only those pesticides and food additives which are safe and do not create a health hazard are put on to the market. The process at the moment of registration and control is an often haphazard one
involving Agriculture Canada, Health and Welfare and provincial agencies.
There has been a good deal of criticism of the way in which both the risk benefit analysis has been carried out, the concentration on risk benefit analysis, and on the resources available for ensuring that effective controls are in place.
The Auditor General recently criticized the process of testing for pesticide residues, concluding, in part, that for many products the Department of Agriculture does not know the extent of human health risks posed by chemical and bacterial contamination in these foods and cannot assure itself that its inspection resources are directed to where these resources are greatest.
I would like to raise one other concern about the present situation in which we find ourselves with regards to the regulation of pesticides and food additives, in particular dealing with pesticides and then perhaps make a couple of suggestion.
This already difficult situation with regard to the registration of pesticides and the enforcement of pesticide control and food additive control has been extenuated by Schedule 7 of the free trade agreement which Canada recently signed with the United States. Schedule 7 deals with pesticides and with a move towards the equivalence of standards. Schedule 7 requires that there be work toward equivalent guidelines, technical regulations, standards and test methods; that there be work toward equivalent residue monitoring programs; that there be work toward equivalent technical regulations, standards or certifications for those pesticides; and work towards equivalence and the process for risk benefit assessment, tolerance setting and the setting of regulatory policies with respect to certain pesticides.
Canadian standards tend to be more rigorous than those in the United States, and the government has agreed, through this process of equivalence, to begin the process of reducing our standards and thus the degree of protection available to Canadians. At least, in this particular schedule, the free trade agreement does not talk about harmonization, but it does talk about equivalence, the bringing down of those standards.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Or the raising up by the Americans.
October 5, 1989
Well, it is very unlikely that we are going to see the Americans raising their standards to our standards.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Why?

The
number of producers in the United States is significantly higher than the number of producers in Canada and the number of products available is significantly higher than those available in Canada.
What we need is a new method of pesticide registration to ensure that questions of health and environmental effects are more effectively put into the technical and economic equation. The costs and risks of pesticide use must be determined and research must be conducted into additive effects of chemicals on the environment, the users, and the consumers.
Users and consumers must be fully informed of the risks they face, and that includes adequate labelling of pesticide products to include health assessments. Food labelling must also include additives and the probable presence of pesticide residues in food irradiation. All those things would assist in ensuring that consumers are well aware of the procedures to which their foods have been subjected.
It would be useful also, as many have called for, if the government would create a new classification for fresh and processed foods which are pesticide free or organic foods which ensure that the consumers are well aware of the lack of presence of pesticides in some of the products that are available.
One of the serious problems that has arisen with regards to pesticides and chemical additives, as raised in the motion, is that we have very little knowledge of the cumulative effect of the various pesticides and chemical additives in our food today. There is a notorious chemical soup of products and additives out there and we really have very little understanding of how they all fit together.
Tests which are generally conducted are tests about the toxic nature of one product being used alone, separate from all others. What scientists see from these toxicity studies is the specific result of using just one chemical, one pesticide, or one additive. What Pollution Probe has called for is a significant exploration of the
Private Members' Business
interaction between chemicals and the total chemical load on the population from pesticides, food additives, and the seemingly endless list of industrial chemicals that are available.
The number of pesticides alone is formidable. More than 600 of them are used throughout the world and about 220 are currently approved in Canada. Because so many factors, including pesticides, chemical additives and many other things that are present in our environment, contribute to the health difficulties that people face, we need another way of assessing toxicity and of testing for chemicals other than just concentrating on one single commodity at any given time. There are many things that the government could do to place a higher priority on the health of Canadians in this context.
As I have mentioned, first of all we need a more public process for the assessment of regulating pesticides and food additives and we need to ensure that we not only perform risk benefit considerations, that we do not face off health and economic matters, but indeed that we ask the real questions as to what risk these products give rise to.
We must pay particular attention to the compounding effects on all of the various chemicals utilized at different stages of our food production process. We must find out what is happening. We must conduct research on the cumulative effects of food additives and chemicals. This would be a critical step to take.
In conclusion, I would say that the government should take action on this immediately.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposal before us today is to consider whether the government should undertake research on the cumulative or combined effects of food additives and pest control products in the Canadian food supply.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure all members of the House are aware, rigorous controls are in effect with regard to both pesticides and food additives. For example, pesticide products are registered in Canada under the Pest Control Products Act. This act is administered by Agriculture Canada with registration of products occurring only after extensive consultation with various other government departments, including the Department of National Health and Welfare, and Environment Canada.

October 5, 1989
Private Members' Business
Health and Welfare evaluates the safety of these pest control products, both for the potential hazards of residues in foods and for occupational exposure risk to workers using these materials. Unlike the registration systems in some other countries, the Canadian registration process is extremely rigorous and places paramount importance on the safety of the pest control product both to the users and consumers of foods treated with these substances.
Residues in foods are regulated under the Food and Drugs Act and regulations through the establishment of maximum residue limits. Such maximum residue limits incorporating substantial built-in safety factors are set as low as possible and are based on both safety considerations and good agricultural practice.
Over the years, the increase in scientific knowledge, coupled with the evaluation and re-evaluation of pest control products has resulted in Canada enjoying one of the safest food supplies in the world. New pest control products are subjected to more and more stringent evaluation while older products such as DDT and Alach-lor exhibiting definite or suspected safety hazards have been removed from the Canadian marketplace.
This strict evaluation process, in conjunction with the maximum residue limits under the food and drug regulations have shown positive results in the national pesticide monitoring survey, which indicates that a very small number of violative residues are being found in foods. In addition, the ongoing Canadian market basket survey indicates that the majority of foods consumed by Canadians contain little, if any, pesticide residues.
It must be kept in mind, however, that the food supply is, in fact, a collection of chemicals, such as proteins, minerals, vitamins combined in a variety of ways. Many of these chemicals are eaten in concentrations much higher than the residue levels of pest control products. It has often been stated that some of the naturally occurring chemicals are much more toxic than most of the pest control products in use today. If these natural chemicals were subjected to the same rigorous evaluation as the registered pest control products, it is possible that portions of the Canadian food supply would disappear.
Because of the vast number of chemicals and the multitude of permutations and combinations of interactions involved, a study of all possible combined effects of selected substances would be virtually impossible to carry out. It would also be extremely costly.
It also to be borne in mind that foods have been eaten for centuries with little evidence of any cumulative or combined effects. One therefore wonders when the residues of the pest control products are so low in comparison to other naturally occurring chemicals, what additional benefits for the consumer would arise by a study of the cumulative or combined effects of this group of compounds either singly or in possible combination with other substances such as food additives. This is particularly questionable in the face of no substantial evidence of existing hazard.
As I mentioned before, the available monitoring data indicated that the use of pest control products in Canada generally results in residues which are either non-detectable or at levels well below the established maximum residue limits established under the Canadian food and drug regulations. Furthermore, there is no scientific evidence to suggest that Canadian consumers have been exposed to hazardous or harmful pesticide residues in food as a result of the legal use of these products.
In fact, over the past three decades, there has only been one case of pesticide poisoning due to contaminated foods. This case, which was handled by regulatory authorities, was due to an illegal use and resulted in only temporary discomfort for the consumer involved.
Another fact to consider is that the majority of the pest control products sold in Canada are herbicides which are used for weed control. These herbicide products are generally applied very early in the growing season and therefore usually result in very low, if any, residues at time of harvest. Based on these considerations, together with analytical data on residues, the potential for the cumulative or combined effects of chemicals in foods to produce adverse consequences is, indeed, relatively small.
It is also important to note that the Canadian diet is very diverse and it is very unlikely that an individual would eat the same food every day without fail for his or her lifetime. Even so, the scientists in health and welfare assume this to be the situation when establishing maxi-

mum residue limits in order to determine the worst case estimates of intake.
I would like to repeat that, Mr. Speaker. It is important to note that the Canadian diet is very diverse and it is very unlikely that an individual would eat the same food every day, without fail, for his or her lifetime. Even so, the scientists in health and welfare assume that this is the case and that that is the situation that exists when establishing maximum residue limits in order to determine the worst case estimates of intake. This procedure, therefore, provides an additional margin of safety for the consumer.
It is also of interest to focus on the question of the cost of the studies which have been suggested by my hon. friend. The best information from private companies and national organizations involved in the pest control product industry indicates that the cost of development of a new pest control product in Canada is $30 million to $60 million and represents at least seven years of intensive research. The cost of the toxicology assessment portion of this data package represents an estimate $8 million to $10 million. These costs are borne by the industry interested in marketing a given product.
To suggest, therefore, that the Canadian government undertake research on the combined or cumulative effects in the pesticide area, which would cost millions and millions of dollars, would certainly be a tremendous burden in an era of restraint, particularly when no substantial benefits to the consumer would likely result.
In summary, there has not been any substantiated reports of combined or cumulative adverse affects in humans due to pesticide residues in food with or without other components such as food additives. The products used on any one crop are generally diverse and do not have the same mode of toxic action. The residue levels of pest control products in the Canadian food supply are generally very low or non-detectable. Acceptable daily intake levels, which are determined for individual chemicals based on extensive toxicity tests on laboratory animals, have built-in safety factors.
Private Members' Business
All of these facts lead this government to believe that this motion and its potential for expenditure of millions of taxpayers' dollars and years of government research manpower is not supported by a real need.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today asks us to consider whether the Government should undertake research on the cumulative or combined effects of food additives and pesticides in Canadian food products.
The Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare is responsible for monitoring pesticide residues in food and the use of food additives.
These chemical substances are currently subject to a comprehensive assessment process before they are approved for use in Canada. At this point, it would be useful to take a brief look at the assessment process, especially where pesticides are concerned. A similar procedure is also followed for additives.
The term "pesticide" includes a whole range of products such as insecticides, fungicides and herbicides.
In the case of most of these product categories, progress made in chemical research during the past twenty years has led to new types of compounds with enhanced specificity, reduced persistence in the environment and lower toxicity for mammals. In many cases, enhanced specificity has meant a reduction in the quantities involved, selective application and lower concentrations of residues in food crops treated, at the time of harvest. Nevertheless, food may contain low concentrations of pesticide residues, and the Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare is responsible for evaluating the potential dangers of these residues and establishing, if necessary, maximum limits in accordance with Canadian food and drugs regulations. We may point out that the presence of pesticide residues is not necessarily harmful to consumers.
Maximum residue limits are established only after a complete assessment of various toxicological tests that are used internationally. These tests include studies on acute toxicity, both short and long term, and are carried out on various animal species in order to investigate a wide range of possible harmful effects, including cancer.

Private Members' Business
The daily admissible dose for a pesticide has a built-in safety factor that allows for the kind of toxicological effects observed in the animal species tested. The daily admissible dose represents that quantity of pesticide that may be ingested daily during a lifetime, without harmful effects. This figure is used to determine the safety and appropriateness of the suggested maximum limits.
The use of pesticides in Canada is based on the principle that the quantity of pesticide applied to a food crop should be the minimum that is required for effective control. Maximum limits are established after analysing the data on residue obtained through tests in real conditions based on the worst case estimate of intake in other words, one tries to obtain the strongest concentrations that could be expected under typical conditions of use. The maximum residue limit represents the maximum quantity of a given pesticide that may legally be found on a given food product. These limits are usually established using a whole, unprocessed agricultural product at the time of harvest, which may be seen as an additional safety margin. Since the concentration of many residues decreases during storage and transportation, and of course when the food is washed, ground and cooked, the residues in many cases fall well below the maximum acceptable limit and frequently are not detectable.
To enforce the food and drug regulations, the Health Protection Branch continually monitors Canadian and imported food. This surveillance shows that generally food contains pesticide residues in concentrations well below the maximum thresholds. In the rare cases where violations are found, they are mainly due to the use of a pesticide on a crop not being registered in Canada, although in some cases, higher upper limits had been authorized for the same pesticide on other food products. When violations are brought to light, appropriate measures are taken, including recall of the food product, Mr. Speaker.
The statement that actual pesticide residues are well within the statutory limits is also based on the preliminary results of the most recent comprehensive diet study conducted between 1985 and 1988 by the Department of National Health and Welfare. This study makes it possible to estimate the proportion of chemicals in humans from an analysis of these substances in composite samples of representative foods in the average total food intake of the population. The samples analysed are
obtained in the marketplace and prepared for use just as in an average home kitchen.
Preliminary results confirm previous findings that any pesticide residues are in concentrations well below the statutory limits and that for the most part, they represent only a small fraction of the allowable daily dose calculated by the Health Protection Branch.
Mr. Speaker, no pesticide can be considered absolutely safe, but it is important that this danger be linked to exposure.
As was mentioned before, the mere detection of a small dose of such a substance in food does not mean that this substance is necessarily dangerous. Indeed, some common garden vegetables naturally contain substances that produce significant toxic effects in laboratory animals when administered in high doses.
In some cases, the concentrations of these vegetable substances is higher than those reported for synthetic pesticides or food additives. In any event, no data lead us to believe that eating such food as part of a well-balanced diet can endanger consumers' health.
Before beginning research on the cumulative interactions and potential combined effects of these residues in low concentrations with other substances in food, we should first consider Canada's safety record over the last 20 years. No death or illness due to pesticide residues in legal amounts has been recorded. Indeed, the only proven death resulting from the consumption of a pesticide residue in food that was recorded in Canada was due to the illegal use of a veiy highly toxic pesticide on cucumbers.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, since the recorded concentrations of pesticide residues in Canadian food supplies are very low and Canada's food safety record with respect to these substances is excellent, doing research into the cumulative or combined effects of pesticides with other substances such as additives in Canadian food products does not seem a priori to be a priority for now or likely to become one.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing has in a very thoughtful speech put before us this afternoon this question of what happens when food additives and pesticides that are about us everywhere and in the food
October 5, 1989

chain combine one with another. What is the cumulative effect, the cascading effect, of more and more of these being added.
Given the fact that over 5 billion of us humans not to mention hundreds of billions of other animal and life forms are taking nourishment in various ways throughout every single day, there is no question but that this topic is one of central importance and in some respects relates to survival, because nourishment is what sustains life in all its forms.
I was glad to hear him take a thoughtful and essentially non-partisan approach in bringing this subject to the floor of the House this afternoon. I can, I guess, overlook a couple of areas where bias got into his remarks, where he felt he had to condemn the government and also take a side-swipe at the Americans and the free trade agreement.
I only want to say that I think Canadians expect parliamentarians to deal with issues of the environment in a way that is beyond partisan politics. There are certainly times and issues on which there will be differences in party opinion, differences of ideology, but in effect we have something here that, like several other issues in our country and at the international level, really are of transcending importance. Most Canadians that I know do not care what a party platform is or what a personal partisan drive is on an environmental issue. They want to hear answers that are concrete and specific.
To do that, I would first like to elaborate on the hon. member's plea to the government for a more public process and begin by referring to action that is now under way this year in the formation of the Federal Pesticide Registration Review Team.
This document which relates to the current activities of this Pesticide Registration Review Team has three points in it that I would like to mention fairly briefly. The first has to do with who are the members of this team. There are representatives from consumer groups, environmental groups, the farming community, labour, public health, biological, federal regulatory agencies, the forestry sector and the pesticide industry. It is a completely balanced, comprehensive and representative
Private Members' Business
team of people to be involved in any review of pesticide use and registration in Canada.
The second point relates to a statement of purpose of this body. It is very brief, admirably expressed in one sentence, as follows:
Recognizing the principles of sustainability, the purpose of the Review Team is to formulate recommendations for the Minister of Agriculture to adapt the Pesticide Registration process to changing policies and conditions with a view to ensuring the efficient federal regulation of pest control products that minimize the risk of harm to human health and the environment while meeting the needs of the stakeholders.
The third point that I would like to extract from this document for the purposes of the debate this afternoon is to note that as a result of their very first meeting earlier this year-this group continues to meet actively-20 separate issues were identified as constituting their initial focus. We are beyond the stage here of dealing with general statements or good intentions. We are down to dealing with very specific aspects of Canadian policy dealing with pesticides.
The issues include having a clear and central focus on where the federal decision-making authority for regulating pesticides is located; the extent and cause of backlogs in registering new products; the effectiveness of the existing Minor Use of Pesticides Program; the role of risk management principles in making regulatory decisions; the role of the public in the registration process.
Others include the co-ordination and co-operation with the provinces; co-ordination and co-operation between Canada and the United States; co-ordination of pest control products regulations with the important new legislation, Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System; enforcement program and penalty provisions; research permits; labelling; an ongoing review mechanism to ensure that the regulatory process can adapt quickly and fairly to changing needs and conditions. So it goes.
I am not reading all of this into the record but I did want to take the occasion to raise that for the consideration of members, particularly the member whose motion is before the House now, to indicate that this is not something that is new. This is not something that has caught the government by surprise, it is an issue that has for years been of central importance to Canadians, including previous governments. That is why Canada has had very strict and high standards relating to food, to consumer labelling, to ingredient identification. There is a separate issue that is somewhat related to this subject. We currently have a problem in Canada, and I believe

October 5, 1989
Private Members' Business
the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was responding publicly to it today, of American products coming into Canada that do not comply with Canadian labelling requirements. For example, there are boxes of cereal on which the Americans talk about cholesterol, but we cannot in this country even use that word on a product. There are many Canadian standards that are much higher and stricter which I would speak of if I had time, but perhaps another member can pick up this point.
I want to deal with the procedure that is followed in Canada for testing food additives, approving them and controlling them, because Canadian standards in this area are very high. Frankly, the member is promoting further research. I do have significant reservations about research which involves animals for testing. I recognize that medical research is very important in that area, but there are a lot of other areas of testing where I think we have to look with more care than we have in the past as to what we wish to subject animal populations to in the name of some form of research.
This is something that two other members of the House and I are currently investigating, the various animal testing laboratories under the aegis of the federal government. I will leave it to another speaker to go into that procedure in detail, but the result of that procedure is that Canada has the best record of safety in food on the market of any countiy. We have in fact a remarkable state here that whenever there is some problem with food poisoning, whether it be with the kinds of difficulties that the hon. member was mentioning, it is a cause for great consternation and discussion because it is the exception to the rule.
I think the issue is important but we must be very careful not to raise unfounded fears in this area but to deal with the facts and keep the system that we do have on the track, especially as it can be modified as the result of the work of this review team to whose activities I have drawn attention.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on this private member's motion by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing which reads:
That in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of undertaking research on the cumulative or combined effects of food additives and pest-control products in the Canadian food supply.
I heard the member opposite say Canada has the best record in terms of testing and control for safety. I would submit that a part of progress is always to build on our strengths and to continue on. Research does not mean that we are putting into question the current state of the situation. It means we would like always to work for the health and safety of all Canadians.
People are becoming less and less confident about the adequacy of government regulations limiting drugs and chemicals in foods. The government does not ban fruits and vegetables when it finds low pesticide residues or forbid the dosing of animal meats with hormones and antibiotics. Warnings about tainted food may be issued only when a consumer falls ill, when a citizen becomes a patient. That is too late. That is not prevention.
Several events in the past year indicate that there is good reason for the public to be increasingly concerned about what is in the food they eat. I would therefore like to laud the member who introduced this private member's motion.
In October our own Canadian Auditor General, Mr. Kenneth Dye, questioned the adequacy of government food testing and pesticide-regulating programs in his annual report. So obviously there is room, in fact a great deal of room for improvement.
A study released in February by the Natural Resources Defence Council, the NRDC, in Washington, D.C., estimated that up to 6,200 pre-schoolers in that part of the country may eventually develop cancer because of repeated exposure to pesticide residues on fruits and vegetables. That figure certainly is alarming and is not acceptable to any citizenry, certainly not to Canadian society. The major cause for concern is the pesticide daminozide, known by its trade name Alar.
October 5, 1989

The Ontario government released a study last September that concluded that dioxins and furans, two families of toxic substances, can be found in low levels in many foods, including meat, poultry, wheat, eggs, fruits, vegetables and milk.
Now I would like to speak more about the pesticides. Federal government officials estimate that between 250 and 300 pesticides are in use. Pesticides are sprayed on fruits and vegetables and kill parasites, fungi and weeds. They help to ripen produce, improve its colouring and protect it from bruising.
Agriculture Canada states that about half of fruits and vegetables have residues below the tolerance level, and most meat products also contain minute traces of pesticides. But Diane Kirkpatrick, Director of Health and Welfare Canada's Bureau of Chemical Safety, says that while the government should remain vigilant in monitoring levels, unless that is done, consumers may not be safe because residues are below the stated limit. So there is a need for continuing research. There is a need for research into the cumulative effects of additives and food pesticides.
She also said that the government is not worried about minute levels of Alar on apples and that there is no concrete evidence from animal studies as yet that Alar is carcinogenic. But there is a principle in law: "Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence". We would not like to wait for the harm to happen. When we have demonstrated the harm, even in animal studies, we have to accept that and presume the safety of the individual is foremost in our minds.
The NRDC study states that Alar is a potent carcinogen. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, while it believes that NRDC's analysis is exaggerated, has, nevertheless, announced it is accelerating its proposal to ban Alar. So there was concern. Yet, Health and Welfare Canada has given the chemical a clean bill of health. So again there is a need for awareness on the part of the Canadian public.
The key difference between the U.S. and Canadian responses is how the governments interpret cancer risks from chemicals. Virtually all the information about the safety of chemicals comes from tests on rats and mice in the laboratory. In the case of daminozide and the chemical known as UDMH-the daminozide breaks down into a compound called UDMH when processed into apple sauce and apple juice-the laboratory studies
Private Members' Business
to date are somewhat ambiguous. After the first year of a two-year study UDMH caused cancer in animals only at the highest dose tested. Canadian officials have interpreted this information to mean that UDMH is only carcinogenic when consumed in very large quantities.
By contrast, U.S. officials believe that, despite the uncertainties, there is a good chance that UDMH increases the risk of cancer even when consumed in much smaller doses.
I think the message here is, at a given point in time a particular dose of consumption may not be harmful. When taken over a period of time, cumulatively, it could harm the citizen.
The Environmental Protection Agency estimates that the levels of UDMH found in apple products present a lifetime cancer risk of about one in 22,000. Now, if you look at the risk of diseases in medical practice, certainly we worry even when the risk of illness is one in 22,000. We try to discover a cure. We try to discover a treatment. So if we do that in the day-to-day practice of medicine, then certainly we should also be concerned about risk of cancer even if the studies are not quite definitive yet.
Although this is a minute risk for each individual, when averaged over an entire population, however, it appears much more significant.
The Environmental Protection Agency's analysis is correct. UDMH could cause about 1,000 additional cancers in a nation the size of Canada. That is alarming. The key question is what to assume for the purposes of a regulatory policy. This is where Canada's approach is disturbing. The U.S. assumptions are the most protective of health, while Canada's are much less so. If Canada is wrong there will be continued exposure to a cancer-causing chemical and an increase in deaths due to cancer.
The University of Western Ontario Geneticist, Dr. Joseph Cummins worries that a pesticide like Alar might cause rare blood vessel cancers and thus there will be a measurable increase in that kind of cancer in the future.
Linda Pim, a Toronto environmental biologist, has similar concerns about the long-term impact of pesticides. Although individual chemicals might be safe on their own, they might be dangerous in combination with others. Again, this is one aspect of harm that research as proposed by this motion could show the Canadian public and our Canadian health officials. I would say that the

Private Members' Business
government does not seem to appreciate the seriousness of these concerns.
I thought I could discuss the dioxin and furans, the two toxic families of chemicals, but I will respect the time you have allotted me and conclude that the government should place much more emphasis on the health of Canadians. If it did, it would be more concerned about the potential ill effects of pesticides, hormones, antibiotics and dioxins and furans. There is a need for more testing to be done to determine what levels of the substances are harmful and a corresponding review of the regulations which control their use.
I support this motion. When we determine to do research, when we tiy to establish what potentially could harm the Canadian public, there can only be progress, and therefore, I support this motion. I would like to ensure the continuing safety of Canadians through research.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing (Mr. Axworthy). The motion before the House today deals with a very complex technology, namely the analysis of non-harmful food ingredients such as additives and pesticides, a field that is highly specialized. The aspects of this motion which concern food additives could be used to illustrate the degree of complexity involved. Actually, it would be preferable to separate the cumulative effects from the combined effects of food additives, simply because these are two entirely different matters.
The comprehensive toxicological assessment that food additives undergo before their use in Canada is approved will provide most of the information on the so-called cumulative effects of these products in the human body.
Food additives are no different from other chemical products that enter the body and are used by the body, and more specifically, the myriad of chemical products contained in food which include proteins, carbohydrates and fat. Some are transformed by normal bio-chemical reactions as a result of the body's metabolism and can help the body produce energy, while others, because of
their physical and chemical properties, may never be absorbed and remain basically unchanged after entering the body.
Others may be absorbed and subsequently eliminated.
Actually, the human body is a wonderfully effective machine that is constantly ingesting food, water and air and uses what it needs while getting rid of the rest in one way or another.
We can say that relatively few elements have a chance to accumulate in the body. Usually they are either used or eliminated. If food additives were to accumulate and if such accumulation were to have a toxic impact, this would be detected by the toxicological analyses that are standard for all food additives before they are approved for use.
If these studies showed signs of accumulation, a thorough assessment of the significance of these findings would be done before the additive could be approved for use in food.
To examine the somewhat more complex issue of the combined effects of food additives, we have to consider the thousands of chemical products to which the body is exposed when it ingests food.
If we add one or two food additives to this whole mixture of chemical products that naturally occur in food, we must not conclude that these additives will necessarily set off a toxic reaction.
In fact, the odds are there would be a much higher risk that some of the thousands of other chemicals products would react together. That is what happens in cooking, Mr. Speaker, when we prepare food.
In fact, it is difficult to predict all the reactions that can be generated by food ingredients, including additives.
However, just as when other food elements or additives or pesticides are involved, this issue is dealt with by chemists, nutritionists or professional toxicologists with the Department of National Health and Welfare, during the strict pre-approval process.
As you know, research in this area would not be particularly useful. Most of the food we eat is cooked, which brings about hundreds and thousands of changes.
October 5, 1989

However, cooked food is eaten every day, and food is cooked for health reasons, because this rids the food we will eat of micro-organisms that can cause problems in the area of public health.
If we were to have a research program on the combined effects of food additives, we would have to ask ourselves several questions, like: Were do we start? What combinations of additives must be considered? How should these combinations be studied? Perhaps some other benefits that the consumer might derive should be considered as well. And last but not least, what would such a study cost?
It must certainly not be concluded, Mr. Speaker, that such studies are not important in cases that can be easily identified and where the danger is known. However, there would be little interest in beginning an intensive research program to study all possible reactions.
Furthermore, it is not obvious that the reaction products would necessarily be toxic.
They might very well be quite harmless and be handled by the body almost like other food components such as proteins and complex carbohydrates that make up the food we eat every day and which the human body metabolizes without difficulty.
Mr. Speaker, food safety research is a very costly exercise requiring highly specialized scientific personnel and complex equipment worth hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Before beginning such a research program, a thorough analysis of the need and cost-effectiveness must be done to ensure that scarce funds are well spent.
Research on the food supply is and must be based-

Mr. Speaker, this government, through neglect of duty and abuse of staff, is building up a brand new refugee backlog crisis which may end in further injustice to refugees.
On May 9 of this year in Question Period I pointed out to the minister that her new system of refugee determination started on January 1, 1989 was breaking down. Of 2,806 cases opened in four months only 1,008 had received final decisions. The minister answered that the problem was just a matter of start-up troubles. She claimed she would, and I quote:
-continue to ensure that there are enough resources available so the system will work well-
It seems she did not provide the resources. According to the report of the Immigration and Refugee Board for September 11, 1989, of 7,203 cases opened, only 3,243 cases received final decisions-only 45 per cent. The rest, 3,691 cases, are deferred at one stage or another. The pipeline is filling up fast.
There was a time when 2,000 or 3,000 cases was a dreadful backlog. We now have about 100,000 cases in the old backlog, mostly built up since 1984. How many more thousands will this government add in a new backlog?
There is a very plain reason for much of this breakdown-understaffing of the clerical work. This was an important part of the origin of the old backlog, understaffing of the clerical work. It then took three to six months to type a transcript of a hearing under oath and send it to the old refugee status advisoiy committee. So the backlog was launched. As it snowballed, the racketeers found the delays very profitable for bringing in bogus refugees just to benefit by even a couple of years of work in Canada before they would be sent away.

October 5, 1989
Adjournment Debate
Now this government is doing the same understaffing that may launch a new round of racketeering. Appointments are now being made months ahead for hearings which were supposed to be done within a very few weeks. Morale is sinking low in the immigration refugee board support staff, as in the whole immigration department.
After working Saturdays, Sundays and nights overtime, week after week after week, clerks are transferring or quitting. This government, rather than developing a fair hiring policy to meet the need, is resorting to contracting out the clerical work in violation of the union contract. When the government pays a contractor, say Kelly Girl, $900 a week, but the actual girl doing the work gets only $250 a week, not only is the girl being cheated but the Canadian taxpayers are being cheated, and plainly, the work is not getting done right.
Why is this government sabotaging its own pet refugee determination program which it steamrollered through Parliament against massive public opposition?
Last December the minister threatened to apply the infamous safe third country clause of her new Immigration Act if the system began to break down. This is the clause they could use to send refugee claimants into orbit, bounced from country to country without ever getting a fair hearing on a claim. Is the reason the minister is allowing this new backlog to build up to create a so-called new crisis, to justify sending refugees into orbit?
The minister hinted on April 5, according to The Toronto Star:
-she might drop a clause in the new refugee laws that would permit Canada to send back refugee claimants who arrive from a safe third country such as the United States-
I hope she will drop that clause and not use it. The United States is not safe for refugees from fascist governments in Latin America or Africa. They deport most of them likely to prison, torture or death.
Therefore, I call on the minister to clean up her act, to hire appropriate clerical staff for the immigration and refugee board, and to enter a bill in Parliament to repeal the infamous safe third country clause of the Immigration Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have a chance to reply to the Hon. Member for
Trinity-Spadina because he raises this issue as someone who is passionately concerned about the plight of refugees and people who are caught up in the turmoil of bureaucratic procedures. I know that his commitment to the well-being of individuals is one that has caused him to raise this issue now and many times in the past and, no doubt, as long as he is a member of the House, he will continue to bring issues like this before us. It is a reflection of his commitment to seeing that there is justice for all who have anything to do with the Canadian government system.
I think it is fair to say it was that same feeling that motivated the government to bring about changes because of the unacceptable level in the backlog that was developing under the previous operation of the law and the procedures under that law.
The hon. member's concerns-I will not call it an indictment of the new system-that he is already raising about the new system are perhaps not premature but, to be accurate, this new system has been in place only since January 1, and I think there is good evidence as well that it is demonstrating that it can be both efficient and fair, and those two things have to operate simultaneously, I believe.
Claims to convention refugee status certainly are dealt with far more quickly than occurred under the previous process and that efficiency, in turn, is having, I think, at least two benefits. One is that genuine refugees are able to get on with their lives in Canada and, second the abuse by those who have had obviously unfounded claims is being deterred.
The hon. member mentions that 93 per cent of all claims are being referred to the immigration and refugee board and that is absolutely correct. But I think it is important to add that 93 per cent of decisions rendered by the board are to the effect that the claimant is a convention refugee. It was never anticipated that the "creditable basis" test would result in the refusal of a high percentage of claims. Its value has always been seen in its capacity to deter abuse by permitting speedy determination of those claims which lack an arguable base. A more than 30 per cent decrease in claims at ports of entry certainly demonstrates that the test has achieved its objective.
October 5, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I have always felt that there was no point in rising if there is nobody to respond. I certainly would take the answer of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs because his minister chairs the special cabinet committee and he might impose on his minister to pay some attention to the crisis that is developing on the east coast.
My question was to the minister on September 28 at which time the minister in his answer stated:
-on my first review of the report-
This is a reference to the Hache committee:
-it appears that in the present year there are no extraordinary circumstances of hardship which are unlike those of previous years with the exception of lower prices and the problems created by exchange rates.
I can only say that for this minister who has been the minister of fisheries now for a number of years cannot, with his experience, say that there are problems in the fishery this year and last year in the groundfishery is incredible. Municipal leaders said on July 11 that probably 12,000 people are affected directly by the groundfish quotas that were in place under this minister's management scheme. They are worried. They know the problems that will develop because there has been no work. This means that there will be larger welfare rolls because people do not have enough stamps to be able to collect unemployment insurance. There is a spin-off effect with lack of work. It means not enough taxes are collected.
The whole community is affected by the fact that this minister will not look at his management plan and say to the people in the southern end of Nova Scotia, "Yes, there is fish in the waters; yes, you should be able to go out and fish them." The municipal leaders are not the only ones. This week, I got a letter from the Yarmouth County Affirmative Action Committee dated September 15, before the minister's answer, which says that because of the problems the federal government has now instituted regulations which have placed thousands of western Nova Scotians on the unemployment lines. Thousands more cannot now qualify for unemployment insurance. Those are two groups that have directed their
Adjoumment Debate
concerns to this government and they have not been listened to.
In the middle of July, after public demonstrations by the plant workers and the fishermen, two provincial ministers came up and met with the minister. We have had nothing as a result of that meeting. They met again with the Hache committee and said that it was the worst of times and that the management plan was not working. Yet, I do not know what it will take for this minister to start believing people like the member for South Shore who has been saying that there has to be a solution. An awful lot of the fishermen have only had six to eight weeks of work, not even enough for unemployment stamps. Today's paper says "Siddon's comments on fishery called unbelievable by industry". This is in The Chronicle-Herald:
Glen Wadman,, vice president of the Independent Seafood Producers Association of Nova Scotia, said Wednesday the minister's suggestion that there is no crisis in the fishery is "staggering".
We represent 31 independent fish plants, many of whom have workers that have only worked seven to 10 weeks this year-
"Some of them are worried about having their telephones and electricity cut off. Some have had to take their cars back to the local dealers because they're trying to pay for their homes.
To hear the minister make those kinds of statements- well, it's unbelievable.
Others are saying "Let the minister cut his salary by 30 per cent like he cut the quotas of the inshore fishery by 30 per cent". A longliner says, "Soon, because of the policies, they will be tied up." A longliner should never be tied up because it has a fishery that is selective.
I want to say to this House and to the representative of the government who comes from the west one thing. As the Yarmouth County Affirmative Action Committee says, it is noted, and my hon. colleague over there comes from Alberta, "that the federal government did provide extensive assistance to western farmers when drought struck the prairie provinces. The federal government is directly responsible for providing funding for a state of the art fishing fleet". They feel that if one area of the country is going to be helped by this government, why can the other area not be helped as well.
We have waited since the spring to see if there would be an imaginary fund focused on several times by the government saying that there was going to be help for the east coast. Yet we have a minister who says there are

October 5, 1989
Adjournment Debate
no worries on the east coast, there is nothing wrong on the east coast.
There are people who have not worked who normally have had full-time jobs. There are 12,000 people who have worked in Shelburne, Yarmouth and Digby County directly in the fisheries. Over 5,000 of them are full-time plant workers. Let the minister go and tell them that they should not be working.
The worst thing that this Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has done is that he has not believed in the fishermen. He has not believed in the members of his own party who have told him that the state of the fishery is critical and needs to be taken care of and that his management plan is not helping the inshore fishery. He has not listened to the two provincial ministers of the Buchanan government who came here in July and went before the Hache task force and said there was a problem. He has not listened to anyone.
I think it is time that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is the chairman of the special committee, to look at the state of the east coast fishery, and started working as the Prime Minister said he would do to look at the conditions on the east coast. They have not done that. They have sat all summer and allowed a growing problem to exist while they have not listened to the people, the fishermen, the people who know what the conditions of the fishery are on the east coast.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to add to the minister's response that was given to the hon. member for South West Nova. I think it is very unfair for the member to accuse the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans of not listening to members of this House. Indeed he is and indeed he recognizes the problems that are facing the fisheries on the east coast, and on the west coast where we also have problems.
I do recognize, however, the passion and the feelings that my hon. friend for South West Nova has for her constituents. I understand those, coming from western Canada where we have had drought in the past. This is the first opportunity I have had since she came back to the House to publicly welcome her back after a little bit of a holiday-four years. I am glad to see her back. She is a feisty representative.
I will outline a little of what the minister is attempting to do, and I think my hon. friend will understand this also. She knows full well that a task force on the Scotia-Fundy groundfish was formed on July 18, 1989.
The terms of reference for the study were outlined to the chairman, Mr. Jean-Eudes Hache, in a letter from the minister and it includes the following issues: One, the adequacy of existing scientific advice on the Scotian Shelf, Georges Bank and Bay of Fundy groundfish fisheries; two, he wanted to know the basic management principles of the Scotia-Fundy groundfish fishery, including such things as the impact of present harvesting on the resource as well as the different fleet sectors; the effectiveness of conservation controls and an assessment of the capacity of existing fleets; three, the economic impact of alternative fishery management approaches on individuals and companies involved in the fishing industry and communities which are dependent upon the fishery.
The minister directed Mr. Hache to take into account all fleet gear sectors and to pay particular attention to the work and recommendation of the Scotia-Fundy capacity committee, an industry committee which deliberated for approximately one and one-half years on the question of vessel capacity in the Scotia-Fundy fishery. He was further instructed to keep an open mind on all of their options for management as well as to develop alternative approaches to fisheries development, including promotion of conservation-oriented technologies and the exploitation of underutilized species.
The task force began meeting with the industry and the general public on July 18, and completed its hearings on August 31. Some 30 meetings were held across the Scotia-Fundy region from Sydney to Campobello Island. All meetings were open to the public and the press were present at all meetings.
In total, some 61 written briefs were received by the task force as well as many oral presentations.
In addition, numerous suggestions, observations and recommendations were put forward during the open, free and often lively discussions that took place. Little consensus on potential solutions were apparent.
I notice you are giving me the sign to finish, Mr. Speaker. The minister is attempting, with a basis of good knowledge, good understanding and good input from the east coast fisheries, to come up with solutions that will be long lasting and effective. In the meantime, I would

support the member for special support in the interim to help the Nova Scotia and the east coast fishermen over this rough period. I think all members in this House of Commons would agree with me.
IMMIGRATION-INVESTOR PROGRAM-SPECIAL MINISTERIAL PERMITS/GOVERNMENT RESPONSE

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity of discussing and debating during this late show. A question that I posed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration on June 19, 1989, which dealt with the fact that the government had used 100 ministerial permits to extend free entry into this country for people willing to invest under the investor program that was introduced and announced by the government back in 1988.
The problem with that particular action, and who knows if it was repeated in the period between June and the time currently, was twofold. First, the program was amended and announced in 1988. There were expectations created and, therefore, a demand was created, but we have in this House no legislative and formal authority under that new program in legislation. Therefore, that introduces the possibilities, without formal authority in legislation, without proper criteria, for all sorts of abuse with respect to that new program that was articulated back in 1988.
The second problem, of course, is something that has plagued this government's entrepreneurial program which it has doubled since coming into office in 1984. I am not suggesting that there is anything particularly wrong with entrepreneurial immigration as long as there is a fair balance with respect to the other sources of immigration. The big problem is that once individuals get into this country on a supposed plan to invest, create or start a new business or plant, there is very, very little follow-up by this government to see if that plant, business or operation has indeed opened.
There have been many media reports in the last number of months to indicate that people get into this country with a visa on the pretext that they are going to create jobs and set up businesses when in fact those businesses are nowhere to be seen. There must be a way of ensuring that if people are going to build a better mousetrap factory in Edmonton, Alberta, they have to
Adjournment Debate
build that factory, because that is precisely the reason why their visas were extended to them.
The other situation that was very problematic with ministerial permits was the abuse of the principle of a ministerial permit. Traditionally, ministerial permits have been extended to people in very dire need for humanitarian and compassionate grounds. There was no compassionate or humanitarian grounds in terms of dealing with people wishing to invest their dollars and cents. Therefore, there was a double standard at play. People who wanted to invest capital in this country were quickly given ministerial permits. Yet, day after day, in this House and outside this House, we see cases of needy people, facing life or death situations, certainly humanitarian cases, not being able to find the time of day from this minister and this government.
Giving those other individuals special ministerial permits was, in fact, undermining the very concept, principle and tradition of the use of those ministerial permits. It is for that reason and the others that I raised the question in the House of Commons with the minister. We did not get a satisfactory response then and I am looking forward to a response from the parliamentary secretary to try to enlighten this House and those members who are currently in this place to try to arrive at a situation where-
Name them.

Some members are asking me to name them. I have too much respect for the members in the House to begin to name them on national television. We wish to clarify two points in very quick order. The first point is that if the program does not have the legislative authority, why are we proceeding in such an ad hoc fashion.
The second point is that the ministerial permits are traditionally there to help those on compassionate and humanitarian grounds.
Are we prepared to enact the necessary legislation so that this program may be scrutinized by Parliament, given the proper authority, and set up the proper regulations and implement the appropriate criteria under which all investor category entrepreneurs can be, in fact, analysed and processed?

I look forward to my hon. friend giving us the information on these very important matters.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy hearing my friend from York West during Question Period. He knows the meaning of opposition and he handles it very well. I welcome the opportunity to expand upon the reply given by the Minister of Employment and Immigration to the Hon. Member for York West on June 19.
Minister's permits may be issued for a number of reasons, and I think we all know that. In the case of immigrant investors, there are situations where the family with small children would want to arrive early in time for the school year, or to make additional investments in Canada that will contribute to creating jobs for Canadians.
Minister's permits may also be used for other types of situations outside the parameters of the business immigration program, such as humanitarian and compassionate grounds or in the national interest. I think this was outlined by my hon. friend. But I will give an example. A dependant of a person immigrating to Canada may have been found to be medically inadmissible and it has been established that public safety and financial and provincial
jurisdictional factors are satisfactory. It is important to note that minister's permits are being used as a temporary measure for those who genuinely need them, pending passage of regulations or the approval of request for special authority of the Governor in Council.
I would also point out that the minister's permits issued to immigrant investors in 1988 represent .026 per cent of all minister's permits issued in 1988. I want to repeat that, .026 per cent of all minister's permits were issued under the immigrant investor program. That is very, very small indeed.
We are not extending special privileges to the chosen wealthy few, as my hon. friend has suggested. We are simply being fair and equitable to investors as we are to other categories of immigrants.
Finally, I would like to point out that the necessary amendments, as requested by my hon. friend, to the immigration regulations were prepublished on September 9, 1989, and should come into force in the very near future.
